summary: Flaky/RED: web/storefront session-cap tests time out — 20,050 sessions against vitest's 5s default
description:
Found on 2026-08-08 while gating **TKT-198**, and **confirmed pre-existing and unrelated** to it.

`web/storefront/test/session.test.ts` — four cases in the `customer sessions` describe block fail
under `make check`:

```
× bounds the map globally, across unlimited distinct principals   14945ms
× refuses a new session at capacity rather than evicting a live one 8668ms
× lets a customer at their own cap rotate a session even when the map is full 12440ms
× accepts new sessions again once capacity frees up                8060ms
Error: Test timed out in 5000ms.
```

**Proof it is not TKT-198's:** TKT-198's diff is Go and shell only — it touches no TypeScript
(`scripts/smoke.sh`, `services/commerce/internal/bulkrefund/runner_smoke_test.go`, and a new Go
test). With those changes **stashed**, on a tree identical to `origin/main` for all code paths,
`npx vitest run test/session.test.ts` reported **4 failed | 25 passed** in 51s. The gate is red on
`main` for this too.

**Mechanism.** `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL` is **20,000** (`web/storefront/src/lib/session.ts:105`) and
these cases create `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL + 50` sessions each. Every `createSession` does real
per-session token hashing, so a single case does ~20k hashes. `web/storefront` sets **no
`testTimeout`**, so all four run against vitest's **5s default**, and the file needs 15–50s
depending on machine load. Alone on an idle machine the file can pass (observed: 29 passed in
15.6s); under the gate's parallel load it does not.

**Why this is a real defect, not just slow tests.** It fails **open in the other direction** from
TKT-218: a timeout is reported as a failure, so the gate stays honest — but it makes `make check`
non-deterministic on machine load, which means **no ticket can be certified green reliably**. That
is the same blocking property TKT-198 was raised for.

**Conditions of Success:**
- [ ] The four cases pass deterministically under a loaded `make check`, three consecutive runs.
- [ ] The fix does NOT weaken what they prove — the global bound, the refusal at capacity, the
      rotate-at-own-cap path, and recovery after capacity frees. `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL` must still be
      exercised as a real bound, or the reduction argued explicitly.
- [ ] Whether the right fix is a per-file `testTimeout`, a smaller injectable cap for the test, or a
      faster hash in the test path is a plan decision — but note **a smaller cap is a fixture
      change**: ask what the reduced fixture can still distinguish (`AGENTS.md`, "a fixture too
      small cannot show the negative").

**Suggested direction (not a decision):** an injectable cap is the most honest — it keeps the
assertion about the real boundary while making the boundary cheap. Raising the timeout alone hides
that the suite takes ~50s for four cases.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=summary -->
Filed by **TKT-198**'s `agent:coding` stage (gateless run, 2026-08-08) as an incidental: it blocked that ticket's gate but is not its defect. Per the triage rule, incidentals become new backlog tickets rather than scope creep. Not shaped — needs `shaping.md` before Gate 1.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Implementation readiness — READY (shaped 2026-08-08)

**⚠ Gateless run.** Gate 1 waived by the owner along with the other three; shaped and moved to
`Ready` in one step. Same waiver terms as TKT-198 — recorded in the claim comment.

| Criterion | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | OK | Deterministic under load, without weakening the assertions |
| Scope | OK | The test file + a minimal injectable seam |
| Uncertainties | WARN (deferred) | Mechanism choice, alternatives named — a plan decision |
| Dependencies | OK | None; this blocks TKT-198 |
| Approach | OK | **Narrowed during shaping — see below** |
| AC verifiable | OK | Three green loaded runs + a mutation check per test |
| Context-mémo | OK | Baked today |

#### What shaping found, so the plan does not have to rediscover it

**The cost is not crypto — it is quadratic.** The ticket as filed guessed "real per-session token
hashing". That is wrong: `createSession` mints its token with one `randomBytes(32)`, which is
microseconds. The expense is that **every** `createSession` walks the **entire** map
(`session.ts:224-231`) to sweep expired entries and collect the caller's own tokens. Filling to
20,000 is therefore ~200,000,000 iterations per test, four times over. The ticket's own description
should be read with that correction.

**This makes the choice much clearer than it looked:**

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Injectable cap** (recommended) | Removes the quadratic term. Every assertion still concerns the real boundary — refusal at capacity, the global bound, own-cap rotation, recovery — because those are properties of the *rule*, not of the number 20,000 |
| Raise `testTimeout` | Hides that four cases take ~50s. The suite stays quadratic and gets slower as anything else lands. Treats the symptom |
| Make `createSession` cheaper | A real optimization but a **production change** to a security-relevant path, to fix a test. Out of proportion, and `AGENTS.md` warns a bounded/optimized replacement is a new implementation needing its own review |

#### The trap this ticket must not fall into

`AGENTS.md`: *a fixture too small cannot show the negative.* Lowering the cap **is** shrinking the
fixture, so each of the four tests must be re-proved able to fail:

1. `bounds the map globally, across unlimited distinct principals` — needs **more distinct
   principals than the cap**, or it observes nothing. This is the one most at risk.
2. `refuses a new session at capacity rather than evicting a live one` — needs a live victim and a
   genuinely full map.
3. `lets a customer at their own cap rotate...` — needs `MAX_SESSIONS_PER_CUSTOMER` to still fit
   inside the reduced global cap. **A cap below 5 silently destroys this test.**
4. `accepts new sessions again once capacity frees up` — needs room to free.

**The mutation check is mandatory and per-test**: break the behaviour each one pins, one at a time,
observe red, restore. A cap small enough to be fast but too small to fail is the exact defect this
ticket would otherwise introduce while looking green.

<!-- sdlc:stage=ready kind=claim -->
### Claim — TKT-229

**⚠ GATELESS RUN — all four human gates waived by the repo owner**, same terms as TKT-198, extended
to this ticket by the owner's instruction on 2026-08-08 ("do 229 on auto mode first, then resume
198"). Gate 1 was applied at shaping; Gate 2 self-resolved after the cross-model critique preferring
the critique's recommendation; Gate 3 agent-merged after the adversarial review converges; Gate 4
self-validated against test evidence. Recorded so the board history shows this ran gateless.

**Selection reason.** This is the sole blocker on TKT-198, whose own COS 4 (`make check` green three
consecutive times) cannot be met while four `web/storefront` cases time out under load. It also
blocks *every* ticket, not just that one: a gate that fails on machine load cannot certify anything.
Chosen over resuming TKT-198 because merging a gate-trustworthiness fix into an untrustworthy gate
is self-contradictory.

**Risk verdict: `risk:low` NOT claimed.** The diff will likely be small and test-only, which is
exactly the shape that tempts the label. Refused for two reasons:
1. The change makes a **security-relevant production constant injectable** (`MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL`
   bounds a public, unauthenticated flood surface per ADR-049/ADR-051). A seam that lets tests move
   it is a seam that exists in production code, however narrow.
2. The work is **shrinking a fixture**, which `AGENTS.md` names as a defect class of its own — four
   tests must be re-proved able to fail. That is judgement, not mechanics, and on a gateless run
   there is no human downstream to catch a fixture that quietly stopped discriminating.

**Governing ADRs, re-resolved at claim time** (not inherited from the mémo):
- **ADR-049** — customer identity and storefront sessions. The global cap exists *because
  registration is public*; the per-principal cap bounds nothing on its own. Any change here must
  keep that reasoning testable.
- **ADR-051** — public customer surface rate limiting (TKT-224, merged yesterday). The tests
  themselves say *"neither is a fix; TKT-224 is"* — the cap is the last line, not the control. Worth
  reading so the fix does not accidentally re-argue the cap's value.

**Correction carried from shaping:** the ticket as filed blamed "real per-session token hashing".
That is wrong and the plan must not inherit it — `createSession` does one `randomBytes(32)`. The
cost is the **whole-map walk on every call** (`session.ts:224-231`), making the fill quadratic.

**Branch:** `TKT-229-session-cap-test-cost` off `origin/main`. TKT-198's branch is committed at
`3afea81` and untouched.

<!-- sdlc:stage=planning kind=plan -->
### Plan draft — drafted by `gpt-5.6-luna` (config.models.plan)

Run via the codex companion, `task --model gpt-5.6-luna --effort high --background`, READ-ONLY (no
`--write`). The drafter read the real tree before answering. This run was clean — no foreign-skill
hijack, and the state file went `running` → `completed` without the "No job found" false negative
that TKT-198's draft hit.

---

## 1. Decision

Recommend Option A: add a guarded, test-only injectable global session cap and run the four capacity tests with a cap of 40; do not raise `testTimeout` or optimize the production session algorithm.

Option B only hides the quadratic fixture cost and makes future loaded gates slower. Option C changes a security-relevant production path to solve a test-performance problem, requiring a separate design and adversarial review; it is not justified here.

The production default remains `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL = 20_000`. The test seam changes only the threshold used by these tests, not the sweep, per-customer eviction, refusal, or recovery logic.

## 2. Definition of Done

- The four session-cap cases pass deterministically in three consecutive loaded `make check` runs.
- The global-cap tests use the same capacity branch and preserve:
  - a global bound across distinct principals;
  - refusal rather than eviction;
  - own-cap rotation when globally full;
  - recovery after capacity is freed.
- `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL` remains 20,000 in production, with no request, environment, or deployment configuration able to lower it.
- Each of the four tests is mutation-checked, observed RED, then restored and observed GREEN.
- The storefront TypeScript/Astro build passes before the full gate.
- `make check` passes, including lint, tests, builds, and smoke coverage.
- No `testTimeout` change is added.

## 3. Files to change

- [web/storefront/src/lib/session.ts](/home/mathieu/sources/ticketing_system/web/storefront/src/lib/session.ts)
  - Add a private mutable total-cap variable initialized from `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL`.
  - Add a narrowly named `*ForTest` setter guarded to test execution, with integer validation and a minimum of `MAX_SESSIONS_PER_CUSTOMER + 1`.
  - Use the injected value only in the global-cap comparison.
  - Make `resetSessionsForTest()` restore both the session map and the production cap.
  - Keep `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL` unchanged at 20,000 and document that the seam is test-only.

- [web/storefront/test/session.test.ts](/home/mathieu/sources/ticketing_system/web/storefront/test/session.test.ts)
  - Use a local test cap of 40 in the four global-cap cases.
  - Retain distinct-principal fixtures and full-map assertions.
  - Import and invoke the new test seam explicitly in those cases.
  - Keep the existing `beforeEach` reset so the override cannot leak between tests.
  - Add no changes to `vitest.config.ts`, `package.json`, or `Makefile`.

## 4. Test plan

Use `TEST_TOTAL = 40`. The minimum viable cap is 6: five sessions are required to reach `MAX_SESSIONS_PER_CUSTOMER`, and one additional slot is required for a distinct stranger. A cap below 5 cannot populate the customer cap; a cap of 5 has no stranger in the full-map rotation fixture and therefore cannot prove the intended interaction.

### `bounds the map globally, across unlimited distinct principals`

- Fixture: create `TEST_TOTAL + 50` distinct principals, one session each.
- Mutation: remove or bypass the global-cap refusal branch.
- Expected RED: the test observes no `SessionCapacityError` and/or `sessionCountForTest()` exceeds `TEST_TOTAL`.
- Restore: reinstate the global-cap check and rerun the focused test GREEN.

This preserves the reason for the global cap: many principals, not repeated sessions for one principal.

### `refuses a new session at capacity rather than evicting a live one`

- Fixture: create one Alice victim, then fill the remaining `TEST_TOTAL - 1` slots with distinct principals; attempt Bob’s session.
- Mutation: replace the refusal with oldest-entry eviction followed by session creation.
- Expected RED: Bob is not rejected and/or Alice’s victim token no longer resolves.
- Restore: reinstate refusal without eviction and rerun the focused test GREEN.

### `lets a customer at their own cap rotate a session even when the map is full`

- Fixture: create five Alice sessions, then fill the remaining 35 slots with distinct principals; confirm the map is full.
- Mutation: perform the global-cap check before evicting the caller’s oldest session.
- Expected RED: Alice’s rotation throws `SessionCapacityError`, or her oldest token remains live.
- Restore: retain per-customer eviction before the global refusal check and rerun the focused test GREEN.

### `accepts new sessions again once capacity frees up`

- Fixture: create and retain Alice’s session, fill the remaining slots with distinct principals, confirm Bob is refused, destroy Alice’s session, then retry Bob.
- Mutation: make `destroySession` leave the map entry intact, or otherwise prevent the freed slot from being reclaimed.
- Expected RED: Bob remains rejected after Alice’s session is destroyed.
- Restore: reinstate deletion and rerun the focused test GREEN.

After all mutation checks, run the storefront TypeScript/Astro build first, then execute three consecutive loaded `make check` runs.

## 5. Risks

- Mutable test state could leak between cases. Resetting the cap inside `resetSessionsForTest()` and applying the override only in the four targeted tests addresses this.
- The test seam could be misused if exposed through production configuration. It must remain an explicit `*ForTest` export, guarded to test execution, with no request or environment-driven cap.
- The reduced fixture does not measure performance at 20,000 entries. That is intentional: the production default remains 20,000, while the tests verify the same invariant and control flow at a discriminating threshold.
- Production `createSession` remains quadratic when the real map approaches 20,000 entries; addressing that belongs to a separate production-performance/security review.
- The cap of 40 must not be reduced below 6, or the own-cap rotation test loses its distinct-stranger fixture and can no longer prove the intended precedence.

<!-- sdlc:stage=plan-review kind=summary -->
### Plan critique — by `main-agent` (config.models.planReview)

Cross-model pair satisfied: drafted by `gpt-5.6-luna`, critiqued by `main-agent`. Every symbol,
line and seam the draft names was verified at HEAD before judging.

#### Existence checks — all PASS

| Draft claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL = 20_000` at :105, `MAX_SESSIONS_PER_CUSTOMER = 5` at :69 | **PASS** |
| `resetSessionsForTest` / `sessionCountForTest` at :158-165 | **PASS** — and `resetSessionsForTest` currently only does `sessions.clear()`, so the draft's "also restore the cap" is a real, necessary addition |
| `destroySession` exists (mutation #4 depends on it) | **PASS** — :287, and the fourth test already calls it |
| The quadratic walk at :224-231 | **PASS** — confirmed; the fill is O(n²) |
| Four tests at :119, :143, :164, :182 | **PASS** |

#### ACCEPT — the decision, and most of the reasoning

Option A over B and C is right, for the reasons given. Two points the draft got *particularly*
right and which I would have flagged had it missed them:

1. **The derived minimum cap.** It computed 6 from the fixtures (five to reach the per-customer cap,
   one stranger to prove the precedence) rather than picking a round number, and then chose 40 with
   headroom. That is the correct treatment of the shrink-the-fixture trap.
2. **Refusing option C explicitly.** Production `createSession` stays quadratic and the draft says so
   in its own risks section rather than quietly fixing it. Optimizing a security-relevant path to
   make a test fast is exactly the scope creep to refuse.

#### ⛔ REJECT — "guarded to test execution"

The draft specifies the setter be *"guarded to test execution"*. I checked what that would mean
here: **`web/storefront/src/lib/` has no `NODE_ENV` / `import.meta.env` guard anywhere**, and
neither existing `*ForTest` export is guarded at runtime. The convention in this module is the
**name**, not a check.

Adding a runtime environment guard would therefore (a) introduce a bundler/SSR-dependent branch into
a security path for no attacker-facing benefit — anyone who can import the module can already call
`resetSessionsForTest()` and wipe every session, which is strictly worse than lowering a cap — and
(b) diverge from the module's own convention, making the next reader wonder which of the three
`*ForTest` exports is the odd one out and why.

**Amended:** name it `setMaxSessionsTotalForTest`, keep the integer + minimum validation the draft
proposed (that part is worth keeping — it stops a typo'd `0` from silently disabling the bound), and
guard it by convention like its two neighbours. Record the reasoning in the doc comment.

#### AMEND — `resetSessionsForTest` must restore the cap, and the tests must not opt in to that

The draft says reset should restore the production cap, then *also* says the override is applied
"only in the four targeted tests". Both are right, but the load-bearing detail is that the existing
`beforeEach` already calls `resetSessionsForTest()` — so restoring the cap there makes leakage
**structurally impossible** rather than dependent on each test remembering to clean up. That should
be stated as the mechanism, not left as belt-and-braces.

#### CONCUR — the per-test mutation table

Adopted unchanged. All four mutations target the *behaviour* each test pins rather than the fixture,
which is the right shape. Mutation #3 (moving the global check before the per-principal eviction) is
especially well chosen: it is the precedence the code comment at :245-251 says is deliberate, so a
test that cannot detect its reversal is worthless.

#### Pre-mortem — how this ships and is still wrong

1. **The 40-cap tests pass, and nothing ever exercises 20,000 again.** Accepted deliberately, but it
   should be *stated in the test file*, not just the ticket: a future reader must not think the
   suite proves the production bound's magnitude. A comment naming the seam and why is required.
2. **`sessionCountForTest()).toBe(MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL)` assertions.** Three of the four tests assert
   against the imported constant. If a test lowers the cap but an assertion still compares to the
   *production* constant, it fails confusingly, or worse, is "fixed" by loosening it to
   `toBeLessThanOrEqual`. Every such assertion must move to the test cap in lockstep.
3. **The `beforeEach` ordering.** If a test sets the cap *before* `resetSessionsForTest()` runs for
   the next test, the reset restores production and the next test silently runs at 20,000 — slow
   again, and the timeout returns looking like a regression. The override must be set inside each
   test body, after the reset.

<!-- sdlc:stage=planning kind=plan-final -->
### Plan final — delta on the `kind=plan` draft

**The `kind=plan` draft as amended below is the plan.**

#### ⚠ Gate 2 WAIVED — decisions made by the agent

**Decision 1 — Option A adopted, cap 40, minimum 6.** As drafted, including the derived minimum and
the explicit refusal of options B and C.
*Rationale:* the critique accepted it; it is also the most reversible (a test-only seam is deleted
by deleting it, unlike a production algorithm change).

**Decision 2 — the test seam is guarded by CONVENTION, not by a runtime environment check.**
Overriding the draft's "guarded to test execution".
*Rationale:* the critique found `web/storefront/src/lib/` has no such guard anywhere and neither
existing `*ForTest` export uses one. A runtime branch would diverge from the module's convention for
no security gain — `resetSessionsForTest()` is already a more dangerous export and is unguarded.
Following the waiver's "prefer the critique's recommendation" rule. Integer + minimum validation is
**kept**.

**Decision 3 — cap restoration lives in `resetSessionsForTest()`, and the override is set inside each
test body after the reset.** Makes leakage structurally impossible via the existing `beforeEach`
rather than dependent on per-test discipline, and closes pre-mortem #3.

**Decision 4 — every `MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL` assertion inside the four tests moves to the test cap in
lockstep.** Closes pre-mortem #2, which is the most likely way this ships subtly broken.

**Decision 5 — a comment in the test file states that these four cases no longer exercise the
production magnitude.** Closes pre-mortem #1. The suite proves the *rule*, not the *number*, and a
future reader must not have to infer that.

**Decision 6 — production `createSession` stays quadratic; not fixed here.** Recorded rather than
silently accepted. It is a real property: at 20,000 live sessions the walk is 20,000 iterations per
sign-in. Whether that matters is a production-performance question with its own security framing
(ADR-049/ADR-051), and answering it inside a test-speed ticket on a gateless run is precisely the
unreviewed scope creep the triage rule exists to prevent. **Filed as a follow-up rather than done.**

#### Files to change — amended

| File | Change | vs draft |
|---|---|---|
| `web/storefront/src/lib/session.ts` | Private mutable cap + `setMaxSessionsTotalForTest` (validated, convention-guarded); global check reads it; `resetSessionsForTest` restores it | **amended** — no runtime env guard |
| `web/storefront/test/session.test.ts` | Four cases at `TEST_TOTAL = 40`; all cap assertions moved in lockstep; explanatory comment | **amended** — assertion lockstep + comment made explicit |
| `vitest.config.ts` / `package.json` / `Makefile` | **unchanged** | as drafted (no `testTimeout`) |

#### Test plan

The draft's four-mutation table, adopted unchanged, plus:
- **Each mutation run one at a time**, red observed, then restored and observed green.
- **A speed check**: the four cases must complete well inside the 5s default, which is the actual
  point of the ticket.
- Then the TS build, then three consecutive loaded `make check` runs.

#### Introduced at plan-review, reviewed by no second model

Per the required section — these reached the (waived) Gate 2 reviewed only by `main-agent`:

1. **Dropping the runtime guard** (Decision 2). If my reading of the module's convention is wrong,
   this is a deliberately-unguarded mutable security bound in production code. The evidence is
   verifiable (`grep` finds no env guard in `src/lib/`), but the judgement is one model's.
2. **The assertion-lockstep requirement** (Decision 4) and **the leakage mechanism** (Decision 3) —
   both mine, neither in the draft; they are the two ways this ships looking green while broken.

Named again for the ai-review stage to attack.

<!-- sdlc:stage=coding kind=summary -->
### Implementation — by `main-agent` (config.models.implement), commit `97c1895`

```yaml
stage: coding
implementer: main-agent
commit: 97c1895
branch: TKT-229-session-cap-test-cost-v2 (stacked on TKT-198)
diff: +75 / -12 (2 files)
tests_added: 1 (production-default + seam-floor guard)
speed: 15-50s -> 34ms for the four cases
```

#### Mutation checks — all four, one at a time, red observed before green

The substance of this ticket, since lowering a cap **is** shrinking a fixture:

| Mutation | Expected | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| Remove the global cap refusal | all four fail | **4 failed** ✅ |
| Evict oldest instead of refusing | all four fail | **4 failed** ✅ |
| Check global cap *before* per-principal eviction | only the precedence test fails | **exactly 1 failed** — `lets a customer at their own cap rotate...` ✅ |
| `destroySession` becomes a no-op | the recovery case fails | **2 failed** (recovery + the destroy test) ✅ |

Mutation 3 is the one that mattered: it fails *precisely* the test whose comment says the precedence
is deliberate, and nothing else. A shrunken fixture that could no longer detect it would have been
the silent defect this ticket risked introducing.

#### Amendments made during implementation, beyond plan-final

**`MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL` became an unused import** once the four cases moved to `TEST_TOTAL`. Rather
than delete it, I added a test that uses it to assert the production default **is** 20 000 and that
the seam refuses a cap below its floor (and a non-integer). This recovers the one thing the shrink
would otherwise have lost — any assertion at all about the real number — and guards the seam itself.
Not in the plan; called out here for review.

**Deleted an untracked `web/storefront/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo`** produced by running `tsc -b`. It is
**not in any `.gitignore`**, so a stray build artifact is one `git add -A` away from being committed.
Not fixed here (out of scope, and a `.gitignore` edit is a shared-file change); noted as an
incidental for the retro.

#### Gate

`make check` **exit 0** — the first fully green gate in this session. 176 storefront tests pass,
0 migration-race errors.

**Run on a branch stacked on TKT-198** (`97c1895` on top of `3afea81`). Necessary and worth stating:
TKT-229 alone on `origin/main` still fails the gate, because TKT-198's migration race is also on
`main` — verified, 100 race errors with the TS stage passing. Neither ticket can show a green gate
without the other. The stacking is how COS 1 was met at all.

<!-- sdlc:stage=ai-review kind=summary -->
### Adversarial review — by `gpt-5.6-luna` (config.models.aiReview), 3 passes

Cross-model pair satisfied: implemented by `main-agent`, reviewed by `gpt-5.6-luna` via
`adversarial-review --scope branch`, primed for guilt, given the diff only. All three passes
returned `needs-attention` with concrete, line-cited findings.

**Every finding was reproduced before being fixed** — the mutation was applied, the suite observed
passing (i.e. the hole was real), then fixed and observed failing.

| # | Pass | Finding | Verdict | Disposition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | The guard test asserts the *constant*, never the bound `createSession` enforces | **CONFIRMED** — init to 40 passed 30/30 | Fixed → `5ea053a` |
| 2 | 2 | The accessor observes a value *in parallel* with the check that reads it | **CONFIRMED** — `Math.min(cap,40)` passed 32/32 | Fixed → `8ee0631`, one shared `isAtSessionCapacity` |
| 3 | 2 | `beforeEach` turns "the default" into "the post-reset state"; production never resets | **CONFIRMED** — init 40 + correct reset passed 32/32 | Fixed → `8ee0631`, fresh module via `vi.resetModules()` |
| 4 | 3 | Every case uses one `TEST_TOTAL`, so a literal `40` is indistinguishable from the injected bound | **CONFIRMED** — passed 32/32 | Fixed → `e69921f`, second limit at `TEST_TOTAL + 7` |
| 5 | 3 | The fresh-import test cannot detect a cache hit | **CONFIRMED** — proven by dropping `resetModules` | Fixed → `e69921f`, poison the instance first |
| — | 3 | *Refactor to a constructor-injected store* | **REJECTED, stated** | See below |

#### The one rejection, and why

Passes 1 and 3 both recommended replacing module state with a constructor-injected session store.
**Not taken.** It is a refactor of a security-relevant module that every page imports, proposed on a
ticket about test duration — and the narrower fix closes the same hole, demonstrably: the suite now
distinguishes the correct implementation from all five unsafe ones. Taking a structural refactor of
an auth-adjacent module on a **gateless** run, with no human review downstream, is the trade this
run should not make. Recorded rather than dropped.

#### Second pass and the churn cap

Three passes ran. **Not churn — convergence**, which the skill distinguishes: each pass falsified the
*previous pass's fix* at the root rather than re-litigating settled ground, and pass 3's finding #4
existed *because* pass 2's fix introduced the single-`TEST_TOTAL` blind spot. Under the rule "a pass
that invalidates the previous pass's fix resets the counter", a fourth would be permitted.

**Stopping at three anyway.** The suite now kills six distinct mutations and the last pass's findings
were narrower than the first's. A fourth pass on a gateless run is a decision to hand back, not to
take — and the fix diff from `e69921f` is itself reviewed by nobody, which is stated plainly here and
in the review guide rather than papered over.

#### Mutation battery — the standing evidence

Six mutations, each applied alone and restored after; the suite is green with none applied:

| Mutation | Tests failed |
|---|---|
| Initializer set to 40 | 1 |
| Decision hard-capped via `Math.min(cap, 40)` | 3 |
| Literal `40` in `createSession` | 1 |
| Cap removed entirely | 5 |
| Evict oldest instead of refusing | 5 |
| Reset fails to restore the bound | 1 |

#### Methodological note worth keeping

My own pass-2 mutation *missed* finding #4 because it removed the cap entirely (`if (false)`) instead
of fixing it at the test's own value. **A mutation that is too destructive proves less than a
plausible one** — every test notices a cap that vanished; only a discriminating suite notices a cap
that is quietly wrong. That is the same "fixture cannot show the negative" trap this ticket is about,
recurring inside the verification of the fix for it.

binding.rule: A fixture too small cannot show the negative. A bounded or optimized replacement is a new implementation, so ask what the version it replaced would have caught.

governingAdrs.why: Customer identity and storefront sessions - the session map these caps bound. The global cap exists because registration is PUBLIC, so the per-principal cap bounds nothing on its own.
Public customer surface rate limiting (TKT-224). The session cap and the rate limiter are the two halves of the same flood story; the tests say 'neither is a fix; TKT-224 is'.

reference.summary: The four slow cases and the review passes that earned them - each comment names the finding it pins.
createSession walks the WHOLE map on every call (the sweep + per-principal collect), so filling the cap is O(n^2) - this is the cost, not crypto.
Existing test seam convention in the same module: resetSessionsForTest / sessionCountForTest.

scope.note: web/storefront/test/session.test.ts and whatever minimal seam in src/lib/session.ts makes the cap injectable. Not the cap's VALUE in production, not the rate limiter.

uncertainties.note: Which mechanism: injectable cap (shaping's recommendation), per-file testTimeout, or a cheaper createSession. Named with their trade-offs below; a plan decision, not a shaping gap.

dependencies.note: None. Blocks TKT-198, which is why it runs first.

approach.note: Narrowed during shaping: make MAX_SESSIONS_TOTAL INJECTABLE for tests and drive the four cases at a small cap. The cost is O(n^2) - createSession walks the whole map every call - so 20,000 entries is ~200M iterations. Lowering the cap in the TEST removes the quadratic blowup while keeping every assertion about the real boundary. The module already has a *ForTest seam convention to follow.

first_slice.note: All four cases driven at a small injectable cap, each still asserting the same property it asserts today.

success.note: Deterministic: the four cases pass under a loaded gate, three consecutive `make check` runs, and each test still FAILS when the behaviour it pins is broken (mutation-checked, one at a time).
